BULLYING 2015

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Why has bullying become more inescapable and even more threatening than ever before – Carte Blanche delves deeper.

Summary:
Bullying in South African schools has tripled in the past year. We see more and more videos of teens attacking each other, recording it and proudly distributing the rather disturbing clips.

CARTE BLANCHE BRINGS YOU EXCLUSIVE FOOTAGE OF A BULLYING INCIDENT.

We look into the psychology of bullying, the long term affects and ways of bully-proofing young children.

Further information:
When it comes to bullying there are three key players:
1. The Bully
2. The Bullied
3. And then the Bystanders

OUR EXCLUSIVE FOOTAGE SHOWS THE THREE ELEMENTS IN ACTION.

All have a role to play in the growing trend of bullying. Often we only hear the voice of the victim or the victims parents. Never getting to the source of bullying.


THE BULLIES & THE BULLIED
I hope to get transcripts from sessions with psychologists that have treated bullies – and plan to re-enact them if we don’t get a bully on camera.

I have tracked down the parties in the most recent video - both sides have declined to speak.

ISABELLA HENDERSON – mother of child bullied – video footage of incident

Her 15 year old son was attacked and landed up in ICU in December 2014. He is still being threatened. Some of the teens said he was unconscious for so long and motionless they thought he was dead. There is footage of this - it's quite upsetting.

Isabella is very outspoken about the incident and has tried to make contact with the other families to no avail. She has seen how the incident has affected her own son who is now receiving counseling and has extreme anger issues at home.

WHY ARE WE SEEING MORE BULLYING?
Could it be that there is an increase in aggression, or are we just more aware of bullying because of camera phones and social media.

What role does pack mentality play in these scenarios? And what are the long term affects of schoolground bullying?

What are the solutions: Fight back or Walk away?

EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGIST – still looking for the right expert
We’ll talk about the trend – how it’s changed, how we interact through social media. What the long term affects are of bullying and how it impacts on both the bully and bullied in their adult lives. What drives bullying and are bullies also not victims in their own right unable to deal with social challenges?



STATS – South African Depression and Anxiety Group

- 1 in every 10 learners who drop out of school dos so because of repeated bullying
- 25% of teachers see nothing wrong with bullying and putdowns – and intervene in only 4% of bullying incidents
- over 2/3 of students believe that schools responds poorly to bullying
- bullying is the most common form of violence – 66% of children will be involved in bullying at some point
- 42% of children have been bullied online
- being bullied often leads to depression, low self-esteem and suicide – suicide accounts for 9.5% of all teen deaths in SA

DES BROWN – ANTI-BULLYING TECHNIQUES
Des has been teaching anti-bullying programs to groups of children for more than a decade. His compassion, kindness and deep insight into the effects of bullying have made him very popular with the kids he has taught. With an extensive background in the martial arts, he is also an internationally qualified instructor and group facilitator, as well as an author and speaker.

Des also heads up South Africa’s largest self-defence training organisation, which is represented in Namibia, the USA, and the UK – enabling him to offer unique insight into practical methods of ensuring the physical safety of children in South Africa.

“One of the hallmarks of the BullyPROOF program is that it addresses all facets of self-protection,” says Des. “In fact, learning practical physical self-defence is only one small component of an approach that is designed to completely transform the child. We don’t teach children how to ‘fight’ – although they learn some extremely valuable physical techniques – but really, we teach them how to assert themselves positively. They become confident, purpose-driven, and capable at levels that are absolutely amazing to me.”

Des has first-hand experience of the effects of bullying, having being bullied himself as a child – he remembers the fear, the uncertainty and the sense of hopelessness. For Des, his was created to ensure that kids are empowered to be positively assertive, confident and secure so that growing up can be a time of wonder, curiosity, exploration, learning and fun, rather than scary, uncertain, miserable and bleak.

DEPARTMENT OF EDUCATION
The Basic Education Department says it is very worried about this trend. The Acting Director for safety in schools, Dr Charles Wilson, says bullying can be eradicated, but only if it is taken seriously by the headmasters at schools.

"There are schools that take a very adamant stance against bullying behaviour in schools and then there are schools that are not consistent applying the policy, they sort of brush it under the carpet and those are the schools that we need to focus on."

The Basic Education Department has a generic anti-bullying policy, but several categories of learners must be accommodated. Wilson says cyber bullying, as well as the rights of gay, lesbian and intersex learners must also be protected. He says the Department is working to implement the policy at all schools.

Press Release:


Bully-proof
A recent video depicting serious assault at a Vereeniging school went viral on social media, sending shockwaves across the nation. But this was by no means an isolated incident. According to statistics, incidents of bullying at schools have tripled over the last year alone. What are the dynamics behind bullying on the playground and at the office? Carte Blanche looks into the psychology of bullying, long term effects and ways of bully-proofing young children.


Script:


BULLYING OFFLINE SCRIPT

VO: Flying punches and gut wrenching kicks - feels like an action movie scene. But this isn’t. Globally, bullying is on the rise with more and more videos emerging of violent attacks even from South African schools.

UPSOUND: CELLPHONE VIDEOS

DES: there is a pandemic of bullying, it is subtle, it is widespread and it much more pervasive than people realize.

LINK: With bullying it’s not all the victim and culprit; in essence there are the 3 B’s - the bully, the bullied and the bystanders.

VO: The three make up a so-called triad says clinical psychologist Natalie Solomon.

NATALIE: They all play a role, they’re interconnected and certain the way in which the bully responds, and the victims responds.

VO: Des Brown has been teaching anti-bullying programmes for over a decade. He says it’s often a power play.

DES: the bystander will gravitate towards which ever side is more socially acceptable and right now that is where the bully stands.

VO: This video was taken in December last year. One boy was responsible for the assault.

UPSOUND: Punch // sjoh! Henk!

VO: While at 6 others stood by watching.

ISABELLA: It breaks me till this day to see those videos, I don’t think any mom would want to see her child in that situation. INT 1 M7

VO: Isabella Henderson’s 15 year old son Enrico was invited to a party outside of school. He had no idea that he was the target.

ISABELLA: They wanted to have fun with someone, it was a random pick, they basically invited him with the intention of beating him up.

VO: Enrico ended up in ICU with a concussion later that evening. The video was uploaded to social media almost instantly.

NATALIE: My sense is that it is around a feeling of quite powerful, a sense of control and shaming, the shaming of their victims in a very public forum.

DES: what that does it introduces a new level of bullying where are people are looking in // commenting on and introducing a whole new repetitious cycle of bullying – repetition – so that the incident is not an insolated one – it gets repeated over and over again and that is extremely damaging.

NATALIE: there’s a huge audience that you kind of connect with and there’s no capacity to pause and think about consequences – it’s out there.

VO: But often these viral videos are an example of an extreme blow up – usually, bullying is more constant and subtle intimidation.

Dr. Granville Whittle is from the Department of Education.

DR. WHITTLE: One incident doesn’t necessarily doesn’t constitute bullying. The difficulty with bullying it’s a repeated activity – it can happen over years .

VO: On some level, bullies can be victims too says Des and it is important not to stigmatize them.

DES: All children are victims of their environment and their upbringing – whether you’re a victim, whether you’re a bully, whether you’re a bystander

VO: Veroezka Steenkamp was expelled and criminally charged when this clip of her assaulting a younger Learner went viral.

UPSOUND VIDEO:

DEREK: Do you remember the whole fight or was some of it just a blur?
VEROEZKA: I remember some of the punches, like when I saw the video myself I saw I hit her with the head, I don’t remember that at all.

VO: The victim’s face was cut and her nose cracked.

Now 19 years old, Veroezka hopes by sharing her story that she can help prevent bullying.

She says although it was her first physical fight, she admits that she was bully long before the incident.

VEROEZKA: I could make you feel this small by saying something to you.
DEREK; We talk about bystanders what role do they play?
VEROEZKA: They will say why did you let her get away with it?

NATALIE: the basic human needs and drives are around connections, a sense of value, and importance and recognition in the world. And bullying can connect one with similar minded people. INT 1 M13

VO: Two years later, after 9 court appearances and having faced a possible year behind bars; Veroezka was assigned to a youth diversion programme by the court, 200 hours community service and no criminal record.

DR. WHITTLE: so the psychological impact of bullying is profound – so if you don’t address issues of bullying your levels of violence in your society is likely to increase INT 1 M7

LINK: At times simple teasing can escalate into severe bullying and the consequences can be really tragic…

VO: This Australian video also went viral.

The smaller bully taunts the bigger boy… until he’s pushed too far and retaliates – breaking the bully’s leg.

UPSOUND VIDEO:

VO: Back home, In 2012 – a Gr. 11 victim shot and killed his tormentor in Vosloorus.

And in 2014 a high-school bully was fatally stabbed and another seriously injured in Shosanguve.

NATALIE: I think schools are a microcosm of a macrocosm, //we live in an age of entitlement and very little empathy in that somehow cause and affect are not always linked and we just act.

VO: 21 year old Keagan Calcada says he still carries the emotional scars of bullying. He was bullied from grade 2 all the way through to high school.

Keagan was a smaller, leaner child who took up hip-hop dancing in primary school. His school peers decided that he was gay and started mocking him because of this incorrectly perceived sexual orientation.

KEAGAN: They would throw sandwiches at me during breaks, they would trip me on the way to class, they would push me out of the way. // I could never be part of them – I was the gay kid, I was the faggot, I was the softy, I was different.

VO: Dr. Whittle points out that bullying is not unique to South Africa, it’s a global social phenomenon.

DR. WHITTLE: Bullying levels across the world is very high. It’s about a power relation, so that when you feel someone is different to you and you have more power than that person that’s when the act of bullying can happen,

VO: Often this kind of bullying is not taken seriously. 25% of teachers believe that bullying is not a problem.

In the most recent viral video that shocked the country, a Vereeninging teacher seems completely uninterested by the attack on a learner.

UPSOUND VIDEO:

VO: Dr. Whittle says this s something government is actively trying to address.

DR. WHITTLE: Part of our work as the department is to ensure that teachers understand how destructive bullying can be and the long term consequences of bullying.

VO: A reality for Keagan.

DEREK: how did it make you feel?
KEAGAN: Broken as a person, sometimes I would be lost. It got to the point where I didn’t want to live any more, I tried to commit suicide 4 times

VO: Research has shown the impacts of bullying are long lasting and often permanent, with links to depression and anxiety.

NATALIE: there’s a sense of dislocation, not feeling valued, not feeling important and also a lack of sense of trust – often difficulties with a sense of intimacy

KEAGAN: I think it will stay with me for the rest of my life, self-confidence issues, social issues, social acceptance issues, it’s hard for me to overcome,

VO: Veroezka has learnt the hard way and now realizes the effects of her actions.

VEROEZKA: I know even today…still getting bullied… I just want to sy sorry to her again.

VO: As a young adult Keagan has now found forgiveness for his tormentors.

KEAGAN: but it doesnt take it away, I do forgive them, but I won’t forget, it is something that will live with me for the rest of life. I have got a view in life, where I don't care what you think, I am who I am. Love me or hate me, you are not gonna change me

VO: Kids are told to toughen up, to fight back, to laugh it off – but this is not always constructive says Des.

DES: To draw a realistic comparison would be like me telling a child to laugh off a pedophile, or to tell a woman to simply fight back against a potential rapist. We have equip them with realistic, practical tools, not platitudes,

LINK: When we think about bullying our minds shift from the playground to classroom – when in fact it can be a destructive element in the office and even the home.

NATALIE: where there is social interaction there is bullying - typically as adults it’s not done as kind of a crude a form as children presents, it’s a little bit more nuanced // it’s not quite as straight forward, but certainly it is apparent.

VO: Internationally cyber-bullying has tripled in the last year, a trend that is evident locally too.

DR. WHITTLE Cyberbullying is huge. Countries that have done well to address bullying in schools, have been those countries that have launched particular campaigns to address bullying within their schools.

VO: While it’s an campaign the department is adopting, experts agree that a more holistic approach is needed to cut down on bullying.

DES: There has been a change in the bullying landscape It’s not a person we need to change, it’s a culture. And unless we do something about it now, it’s going to get worse, not better.






PROMOS

PROMO 1 – 10 seconds
VO: Bullies often throw punches while the victims carry the emotional scars.

KEAGAN: I am still broken, I think it will stay with me for the rest of my life,

PROMO 2 – 15 seconds
VO: Viral bullying videos that last
NATALIE: there’s a huge audience that you kind of connect with and there’s no capacity to pause and think about consequences – it’s out there.

PROMO 3 – 15 seconds
VO: With a steady rise in bullying globally - it has become inescapable and even more threatening.

DES: there is a pandemic of bullying, it is subtle, it’s silent, it is widespread

VO: Carte Blanche gets to grips with the bullies

VEROEZKA: I could make you feel this small by saying something to you. DEREK; We talk about bystanders what role do they play? VEROEZKA: They will say why did you let her get away with it? NATALIE: the basic human needs and drives are around connections, a sense of value, and importance and recognition in the world. And bullying can connect one with similar minded people. INT 1 M13 VO: Two years later, after 9 court appearances and having faced a possible year behind bars; Veroezka was assigned to a youth diversion programme by the court, 200 hours community service and no criminal record. DR. WHITTLE: so the psychological impact of bullying is profound – so if you don’t address issues of bullying your levels of violence in your society is likely to increase INT 1 M7 LINK: At times simple teasing can escalate into severe bullying and the consequences can be really tragic… VO: This Australian video also went viral. The smaller bully taunts the bigger boy… until he’s pushed too far and retaliates – breaking the bully’s leg. UPSOUND VIDEO: VO: Back home, In 2012 – a Gr. 11 victim shot and killed his tormentor in Vosloorus. And in 2014 a high-school bully was fatally stabbed and another seriously injured in Shosanguve. NATALIE: I think schools are a microcosm of a macrocosm, //we live in an age of entitlement and very little empathy in that somehow cause and affect are not always linked and we just act. VO: 21 year old Keagan Calcada says he still carries the emotional scars of bullying. He was bullied from grade 2 all the way through to high school. Keagan was a smaller, leaner child who took up hip-hop dancing in primary school. His school peers decided that he was gay and started mocking him because of this incorrectly perceived sexual orientation. KEAGAN: They would throw sandwiches at me during breaks, they would trip me on the way to class, they would push me out of the way. // I could never be part of them – I was the gay kid, I was the faggot, I was the softy, I was different. VO: Dr. Whittle points out that bullying is not unique to South Africa, it’s a global social phenomenon. DR. WHITTLE: Bullying levels across the world is very high. It’s about a power relation, so that when you feel someone is different to you and you have more power than that person that’s when the act of bullying can happen, VO: Often this kind of bullying is not taken seriously. 25% of teachers believe that bullying is not a problem. In the most recent viral video that shocked the country, a Vereeninging teacher seems completely uninterested by the attack on a learner. UPSOUND VIDEO: VO: Dr. Whittle says this s something government is actively trying to address. DR. WHITTLE: Part of our work as the department is to ensure that teachers understand how destructive bullying can be and the long term consequences of bullying. VO: A reality for Keagan. DEREK: how did it make you feel? KEAGAN: Broken as a person, sometimes I would be lost. It got to the point where I didn’t want to live any more, I tried to commit suicide 4 times VO: Research has shown the impacts of bullying are long lasting and often permanent, with links to depression and anxiety. NATALIE: there’s a sense of dislocation, not feeling valued, not feeling important and also a lack of sense of trust – often difficulties with a sense of intimacy KEAGAN: I think it will stay with me for the rest of my life, self-confidence issues, social issues, social acceptance issues, it’s hard for me to overcome, VO: Veroezka has learnt the hard way and now realizes the effects of her actions. VEROEZKA: I know even today…still getting bullied… I just want to sy sorry to her again. VO: As a young adult Keagan has now found forgiveness for his tormentors. KEAGAN: but it doesnt take it away, I do forgive them, but I won’t forget, it is something that will live with me for the rest of life. I have got a view in life, where I don't care what you think, I am who I am. Love me or hate me, you are not gonna change me VO: Kids are told to toughen up, to fight back, to laugh it off – but this is not always constructive says Des. DES: To draw a realistic comparison would be like me telling a child to laugh off a pedophile, or to tell a woman to simply fight back against a potential rapist. We have equip them with realistic, practical tools, not platitudes, LINK: When we think about bullying our minds shift from the playground to classroom – when in fact it can be a destructive element in the office and even the home. NATALIE: where there is social interaction there is bullying - typically as adults it’s not done as kind of a crude a form as children presents, it’s a little bit more nuanced // it’s not quite as straight forward, but certainly it is apparent. VO: Internationally cyber-bullying has tripled in the last year, a trend that is evident locally too. DR. WHITTLE Cyberbullying is huge. Countries that have done well to address bullying in schools, have been those countries that have launched particular campaigns to address bullying within their schools. VO: While it’s an campaign the department is adopting, experts agree that a more holistic approach is needed to cut down on bullying. DES: There has been a change in the bullying landscape It’s not a person we need to change, it’s a culture. And unless we do something about it now, it’s going to get worse, not better. PROMOS PROMO 1 – 10 seconds VO: Bullies often throw punches while the victims carry the emotional scars. KEAGAN: I am still broken, I think it will stay with me for the rest of my life, PROMO 2 – 15 seconds VO: Viral bullying videos that last NATALIE: there’s a huge audience that you kind of connect with and there’s no capacity to pause and think about consequences – it’s out there. PROMO 3 – 15 seconds VO: With a steady rise in bullying globally - it has become inescapable and even more threatening. DES: there is a pandemic of bullying, it is subtle, it’s silent, it is widespread VO: Carte Blanche gets to grips with the bullies Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for BULLYING 2015 (4592) Nicky Troll 27 June 2015

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Why has bullying become more inescapable and even more threatening than ever before – Carte Blanche delves deeper.
metadata.Summary: Bullying in South African schools has tripled in the past year. We see more and more videos of teens attacking each other, recording it and proudly distributing the rather disturbing clips. CARTE BLANCHE BRINGS YOU EXCLUSIVE FOOTAGE OF A BULLYING INCIDENT. We look into the psychology of bullying, the long term affects and ways of bully-proofing young children.
metadata.Further information: When it comes to bullying there are three key players: 1. The Bully 2. The Bullied 3. And then the Bystanders OUR EXCLUSIVE FOOTAGE SHOWS THE THREE ELEMENTS IN ACTION. All have a role to play in the growing trend of bullying. Often we only hear the voice of the victim or the victims parents. Never getting to the source of bullying. THE BULLIES & THE BULLIED I hope to get transcripts from sessions with psychologists that have treated bullies – and plan to re-enact them if we don’t get a bully on camera. I have tracked down the parties in the most recent video - both sides have declined to speak. ISABELLA HENDERSON – mother of child bullied – video footage of incident Her 15 year old son was attacked and landed up in ICU in December 2014. He is still being threatened. Some of the teens said he was unconscious for so long and motionless they thought he was dead. There is footage of this - it's quite upsetting. Isabella is very outspoken about the incident and has tried to make contact with the other families to no avail. She has seen how the incident has affected her own son who is now receiving counseling and has extreme anger issues at home. WHY ARE WE SEEING MORE BULLYING? Could it be that there is an increase in aggression, or are we just more aware of bullying because of camera phones and social media. What role does pack mentality play in these scenarios? And what are the long term affects of schoolground bullying? What are the solutions: Fight back or Walk away? EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGIST – still looking for the right expert We’ll talk about the trend – how it’s changed, how we interact through social media. What the long term affects are of bullying and how it impacts on both the bully and bullied in their adult lives. What drives bullying and are bullies also not victims in their own right unable to deal with social challenges? STATS – South African Depression and Anxiety Group - 1 in every 10 learners who drop out of school dos so because of repeated bullying - 25% of teachers see nothing wrong with bullying and putdowns – and intervene in only 4% of bullying incidents - over 2/3 of students believe that schools responds poorly to bullying - bullying is the most common form of violence – 66% of children will be involved in bullying at some point - 42% of children have been bullied online - being bullied often leads to depression, low self-esteem and suicide – suicide accounts for 9.5% of all teen deaths in SA DES BROWN – ANTI-BULLYING TECHNIQUES Des has been teaching anti-bullying programs to groups of children for more than a decade. His compassion, kindness and deep insight into the effects of bullying have made him very popular with the kids he has taught. With an extensive background in the martial arts, he is also an internationally qualified instructor and group facilitator, as well as an author and speaker. Des also heads up South Africa’s largest self-defence training organisation, which is represented in Namibia, the USA, and the UK – enabling him to offer unique insight into practical methods of ensuring the physical safety of children in South Africa. “One of the hallmarks of the BullyPROOF program is that it addresses all facets of self-protection,” says Des. “In fact, learning practical physical self-defence is only one small component of an approach that is designed to completely transform the child. We don’t teach children how to ‘fight’ – although they learn some extremely valuable physical techniques – but really, we teach them how to assert themselves positively. They become confident, purpose-driven, and capable at levels that are absolutely amazing to me.” Des has first-hand experience of the effects of bullying, having being bullied himself as a child – he remembers the fear, the uncertainty and the sense of hopelessness. For Des, his was created to ensure that kids are empowered to be positively assertive, confident and secure so that growing up can be a time of wonder, curiosity, exploration, learning and fun, rather than scary, uncertain, miserable and bleak. DEPARTMENT OF EDUCATION The Basic Education Department says it is very worried about this trend. The Acting Director for safety in schools, Dr Charles Wilson, says bullying can be eradicated, but only if it is taken seriously by the headmasters at schools. "There are schools that take a very adamant stance against bullying behaviour in schools and then there are schools that are not consistent applying the policy, they sort of brush it under the carpet and those are the schools that we need to focus on." The Basic Education Department has a generic anti-bullying policy, but several categories of learners must be accommodated. Wilson says cyber bullying, as well as the rights of gay, lesbian and intersex learners must also be protected. He says the Department is working to implement the policy at all schools.
